title: Debunking the Debunkers on the Mississippi Miracle
author: Michael Petrilli
summary: Claims that Mississippi's remarkable test score gains are merely an artifact of the state's third-grade retention policy lack credible empirical support. Recent analysis from Kelsey Piper and Karen Vaites demonstrates that the gains are too large and too persistent to be explained by grade retention alone, and Louisiana achieved comparable progress without using the retention strategy. The debate surfaces concerns about college remediation rates and the failures of test-optional admissions policies, while some education leaders propose shifting from demanding more accountability generally toward building better systems that learn from accountability successes and failures.
points: Mississippi's test score improvements starting in 2003 are too large and long-lasting to be explained by grade retention alone, even though retention contributes modestly to the gains.
Louisiana achieved substantial reading improvements without a grade-retention policy, directly undermining claims that retention is the primary driver of test score growth.
Test-based accountability demonstrably improves outcomes but comes with trade-offs including potential curriculum narrowing and isolated cheating in some jurisdictions.
University of California data shows rising remediation needs among college freshmen, suggesting high school grade inflation rather than genuine competency gains in some states.
quotes: For all of these reasons, while weaker students having an extra year to learn to read is almost certainly contributing to Mississippi's scores, it cannot explain Mississippi's gains since 2003 or even much of Mississippi's gains since 2013.

The body of evidence is overwhelmingly consistent with the idea that test-based accountability meaningfully improves student outcomes. For those who want to revive such policies, now would be a good time to shift from demanding more accountability generally to thinking about how to build better systems.

A new longitudinal study shows better outcomes for students in South Carolina's lowest-performing schools, which were subject to state intervention, compared to schools that just barely avoided the sanctions.
University leaders must acknowledge that the test-optional admissions experiment has been an abject failure. Congress should hold hearings examining how these students were systematically failed.
